# Summary

**Data source overview.** This JAIR 2020 article presents Action Schema Networks (ASNets), a neural architecture that generalises convolution to the action–proposition relatedness graph of (P)PDDL planning problems, so that a single set of schema-tied weights defines a *generalised policy* transferable to any problem in a domain. The paper extends the original architecture (position-aware pooling, skip connections, LM-cut/history heuristic inputs), trains it by DAgger-style imitation of a teacher planner, evaluates it against heuristic-search baselines on seven probabilistic/deterministic domains plus 18,300 Blocksworld instances with ablations, and shows that ℓ1-sparsified ASNets become small enough for humans to read and manually verify.

**EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[86]**

*How the instruction set could be improved:* (1) The template assumes a safety-motivated paper; for capability/architecture papers like this one, the instructions should state explicitly how to map "risk" onto reliability/generalisation/interpretability failure modes (I did this, but the mapping is inferential and could differ across extractors, harming mergeability). (2) It would help to allow an explicit **"limitation / negative-result evidence"** validation sub-type, since much of this paper's reasoning flows from failures (Sokoban, Parking, receptive-field bound, PG-RL inefficiency) into future-work interventions. (3) The rule "end paths at validation → intervention" conflicts with future-work interventions that have no validation; an explicit sanctioned pattern "design rationale --motivates(conf 1)--> speculative intervention" should be documented (I used it). (4) A canonical list of edge verbs *with directionality semantics* (e.g. whether `caused_by` means source is caused by target) would remove ambiguity. (5) Guidance on maximum node count for very long sources (this one is ~25k words) would help balance completeness against redundancy.

**Inference strategy.** Explicit content (architecture, training algorithm, ablations, coverage tables, sparsity study) was extracted literally. Moderate inference (edge confidence 1–2) was used only to (a) frame reliability/opacity/dead-end phenomena as top-level *risks* in AI-safety terms, (b) convert stated future work (recurrent/weight-tied layers, lifted architectures, goal-processing networks, formal verification of compiled sparse policies, efficient RL) into low-maturity intervention nodes, and (c) attach the concurrent UCT-guidance result as a deployment-time mitigation.

**Extraction completeness.** All six concept categories are represented on every major pathway: generalisation/transfer, receptive-field limitation and heuristic inputs, imitation-learning distribution shift, teacher suboptimality, risk-ignoring determinised heuristics, execution-time loops and search guidance, grounding/scalability limits, expressiveness limits (quantifiers, goal formulae), evaluation methodology, and interpretability via sparsity. All 106 nodes are connected, principally through the ASNet layer-stack implementation node, the shared relational-structure insights, and the two headline validation nodes (cumulative coverage; 18,300-instance study).

**Key limitations.** Domain-specific numeric results (per-instance cost tables) are summarised rather than nodified; some related-work contrasts (ToRPIDo/TraPSNet/STRIPS-HGN/LatPlan) are only retained where they carry a reasoning step used by the authors; the AI-safety framing of "risk" nodes is interpretive, since the paper itself is a planning/ML methods paper.

    {"name":"Directly optimising trajectory cost with reinforcement learning to surpass the teacher","aliases":["policy gradient training of generalised policies","RL instead of imitation"],"type":"concept","description":"Reinforcement learning would minimise the cost of trajectories actually produced by the policy, removing the ceiling imposed by the teacher's implicit policy, and would also allow value regression or planning-strategy selection objectives.","concept_category":"design rationale","intervention_lifecycle":null,"intervention_lifecycle_rationale":null,"intervention_maturity":null,"intervention_maturity_rationale":null,"node_rationale":"Alternative training rationale; Section 4.1 Training via Imitation Learning and Section 7.1.2."},
